newsitem.title: USA: Sex harassment lawsuit against ex-Astra CEO dismissed.
newsitem.headline: Sex harassment lawsuit against ex-Astra CEO dismissed.

text.p: A federal judge Thursday dismissed all but one claim in a complaint accusing current and former executives of the U.S. subsidiary of Swedish pharmaceutical giant Astra.Ab of sexual harassment.

In an 18-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Morris Lasker dismissed most of the complaint on the grounds that the plaintiffs -- three male supervisors and two women -- had signed settlement agreements with the company barring further action.

The judge acknowledged that at the time former Astra USA Chief Executive Officer Lars Bildman headed the company, women were "picked up ... fondled, rubbed ... and propositioned for sexual intercourse by Astra's top executives."

Lasker also recognized that the three male supervisors who tried to report the matter were eventually fired. But the judge said that, although one "may sympathize strongly with the plaintiffs ... their assertion that it is 'illegal or improper' to settle sexual harassment claims in order to avoid adverse publicity is without foundation."

He added, "Regardless whether plaintiffs' agreements were obtained by duress, plaintiffs have ratified and affirmed their agreements with Astra." The judge noted all the plaintiffs waited between 11 and 34 months to begin their civil action.
He did give the plaintiffs 45 days in which to supply further information on a final charge of defamation against the company.

Of the executives named in the civil complaint, only one, David Frons, is still employed at the Westborough, Mass. company. Astra fired Bildman and two other senior executives in June 1996 amid allegations of widespread sexual harassment at the company.
Bildman remains under house arrest in the Boston suburb of Brookline facing criminal charges of conspiracy, fraud, filing false tax returns and interstate travel in furtherance of prostitution.

If found guilty, Bildman faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine for each count of conspiracy, fraud and interstate travel. He faces up to three years and a $250,000 fine for each count of the tax charges.
